Rachel —

Thanks for taking this RFP slot. As part of our security review we need a focused "worst-case pathway" analysis that describes how an end-to-end compromise could progress through Redwood's multi-tenant inference stack. Specifically, our security and threat teams want: 1) a concise narrative of plausible escalation paths from a compromised user workload to cross-tenant data exposure; 2) the network and control-plane boundaries that prevent or limit blast radius; 3) example configs or ACL snippets showing egress filtering and VPC controls; and 4) tamper-resistant evidence we can include with our audit (logs, signed config snapshots, or SOC2-relevant artifacts).

Target: a short packet (2–4 pages) plus attachments. Do you have an internal contact for providing a minimal topology image and an ACL sample by next Wednesday (2028-07-25)? We also may need a 30–45 minute call to walk the architecture with our threat team.

Thanks —
Anil Suresh
CISO, OrchidBank

Anil / team —

Below is the condensed "worst-case pathway" narrative and the primary mitigations we provide. I kept it intentionally short for inclusion in your RFP packet — we can expand any section during the call.

1) Scenario synopsis (concise):
- Initial compromise: an attacker obtains credentials for a permitted workload (e.g., via stolen API token or malicious container image).
- Lateral step 1: attacker runs code that attempts to enumerate local KV caches and calls internal model endpoints to exfiltrate tokenized content.
- Lateral step 2: attacker leverages an exposed admin/control-plane API (if misconfigured) to list active model variants or request cache dumps.
- Escalation: the attacker attempts to push a model variant or request batch outputs affecting other tenants, or to open egress channels to an external exfil endpoint.

2) Control-plane / data-plane boundaries (how we limit blast radius):
- Strong separation: the control plane (multi-tenant metadata, orchestration) is logically separated from the serving data-plane; control-plane operations require mutual TLS and RBAC.
- Tenant enclosures: per-tenant inference worker pools are tenant-scoped; caches (KV) are namespaced and encrypted with distinct keys.
- Sidecar enforcement: each worker node runs a sidecar proxy that enforces per-tenant egress policies and mutual TLS to the control plane.
- Network microsegmentation: we apply VPC-level routing and security groups to only allow necessary east-west flows; management ports are restricted to the orchestration fabric.

3) Egress and outbound filtering (practical examples):
- Customers can configure allow-lists for external destinations; default is block-all with explicit allow.
- We support granular egress by CIDR/name and port; example snippet (attachment) shows an ACL that only permits outbound TLS to a customer-owned S3 gateway + redwood-update.redwood.ai.

4) Tamper-resistant evidence (what we can provide):
- Signed config snapshots: configs are signed with a Redwood key and include a hash published to an audit log.
- Immutable logs: request and admin audit trails are stored in an append-only store (retention policy configurable per contract).
- Signed ACL sample: we will include a text ACL and a matching signed artifact showing the signature and timestamp.

Quick diagram (very small ascii map):
- [Customer VPC] -- (VPC peering / PrivateLink) -- [Redwood Edge NAT / Egress Filter] -- [Serving pool: tenant A | tenant B | tenant C]
- Control plane (separate) => mutual TLS to orchestration endpoints; operator traffic on dedicated management subnets

Notes / mitigations of interest:
- KV/cache isolation: KV namespaces are keyed per-tenant; encryption keys are rotated and can be customer-managed.
- Canary deployment model: we never promote model code to global pool without staged rollout and rollback thresholds.
- Fallbacks: when workload anomalies are detected, requests are rate-limited and can be moved to a sanitized fallback model to reduce data exposure.

I'll attach a minimal egress ACL example in the next message (Ben will sign it). If you'd like, we can include a short set of config lines showing the sidecar proxy policy for blocking cross-tenant requests.

-Vanessa Ortiz
Director, Security Solutions — Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Worst-case pathway analysis for multi-tenant inference fabric

Vanessa —

This is exactly the level of detail we need. A couple of clarifying asks before we finalize:
1) KMS/HSM: we require that the RFP response state whether customer-managed keys can be used to isolate tenant caches and whether key usage logs are available. We also need the key-id naming convention and a sample audit entry for a key access.
2) Evidence format: for compliance we prefer signed config snapshots published to an immutable ledger (screenshot + signature + timestamp). Will you be able to provide a signed sample (not production secrets) we can reference?
3) Egress flows: when using private (VPC) integration, does Redwood ever route egress via a shared NAT that could cross-tenant? We need a definitive statement.

On the call 07/23 we'll bring our threat ops folks; can you include a brief slide showing the sequence diagram for the escalation steps you outlined?

Thanks —
Anil
